papers.title: Space-time distributions
papers.abstract: The space-time foliation Sigma compatible with the gravitational field g on a 4-manifold M determines a fibration pi of M, pi : M -> N is a surjective submersion over the 1-dimensional leaves space N. M is then written as a disjoint union of the leaves of Sigma, which are 3-dimensional spacelike surfaces on M. The decomposition, TM=Sigma + T^0 M, also implies that we can define a lift of the curves on N to curves (non-spacelike) on M. The stable causality condition M coincides with Sigma being a causal space-time distribution, generated by an exact timelike 1-form omega^0 = dt where t is some real function on M. In this case M is written as a disjoint union of a family of spacelike 3-surfaces of constant t, which cover D^+(S) of a initial 3-surface S of M.

papers.title: A Discrete-Time Attitude Observer on SO(3) for Vision and GPS Fusion
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a discrete-time geometric attitude observer for fusing monocular vision with GPS velocity measurements. The observer takes the relative transformations obtained from processing monocular images with any visual odometry algorithm and fuses them with GPS velocity measurements. The objectives of this sensor fusion are twofold; first to mitigate the inherent drift of the attitude estimates of the visual odometry, and second, to estimate the orientation directly with respect to the North-East-Down frame. A key contribution of the paper is to present a rigorous stability analysis showing that the attitude estimates of the observer converge exponentially to the true attitude and to provide a lower bound for the convergence rate of the observer. Through experimental studies, we demonstrate that the observer effectively compensates for the inherent drift of the pure monocular vision based attitude estimation and is able to recover the North-East-Down orientation even if it is initialized with a very large attitude error.

papers.title: Constrained Geometric Attitude Control on SO(3)
papers.abstract: This paper presents a new geometric adaptive control system with state inequality constraints for the attitude dynamics of a rigid body. The control system is designed such that the desired attitude is asymptotically stabilized, while the controlled attitude trajectory avoids undesired regions defined by an inequality constraint. In addition, we develop an adaptive update law that enables attitude stabilization in the presence of unknown disturbances. The attitude dynamics and the proposed control systems are developed on the special orthogonal group such that singularities and ambiguities of other attitude parameterizations, such as Euler angles and quaternions are completely avoided. The effectiveness of the proposed control system is demonstrated through numerical simulations and experimental results.

papers.title: Family of Controllers for Attitude Synchronization on the Sphere
papers.abstract: In this paper we study a family of controllers that guarantees attitude synchronization for a network of elements in the unit sphere domain, i.e. $\mathcal{S}^2$. We propose distributed continuous controllers for elements whose dynamics are controllable (i.e. control with torque as command), and which can be implemented by each individual agent without the need of a common global orientation frame among the network, i.e. it requires only local information that can be measured by each individual agent from its own orientation frame. The controllers are specified according to arbitrary distance functions in $\mathcal{S}^2$, and we provide conditions on those distance functions that guarantee that i) a synchronized network of agents is locally asymptotically stable for an arbitrary network graph; ii) a synchronized network can be achieved for almost all initial conditions in a tree graph network. We also study the equilibria configurations that come with specific types of network graphs. The proposed strategies can be used in attitude synchronization of swarms of fully actuated rigid bodies, such as satellites.

papers.title: Surveying Graduate Students' Attitudes and Approaches to Problem Solving
papers.abstract: Students' attitudes and approaches to problem solving in physics can profoundly influence their motivation to learn and development of expertise. We developed and validated an Attitudes and Approaches to Problem Solving survey by expanding the Attitudes towards Problem Solving survey of Marx and Cummings and administered it to physics graduate students. Comparison of their responses to the survey questions about problem solving in their own graduate level courses vs. problem solving in the introductory physics courses provides insight into their expertise in introductory and graduate level physics. The physics graduate students' responses to the survey questions were also compared with those of introductory physics and astronomy students and physics faculty. We find that, even for problem solving in introductory physics, graduate students' responses to some survey questions are less expert-like than those of the physics faculty. Comparison of survey responses of graduate students and introductory students for problem solving in introductory physics suggests that graduate students' responses are in general more expert-like than those of introductory students. However, survey responses suggest that graduate-level problem solving by graduate students on several measures has remarkably similar trends to introductory-level problem solving by introductory students.

papers.title: Adolescent Time Inventory-Time Attitude Scale
Adolescent Time Inventory-Time Attitude Scale--Japanese Version
Introducing English and German Versions of the Adolescent Time Attitude Scale
papers.abstract: In this study, the authors report on the development of English and German versions of the Adolescent Time Attitude Scale (ATAS). The ATAS consists of six subscales assessing Past Positive, Past Negative, Present Positive, Present Negative, Future Positive, and Future Negative time attitudes. The authors describe the development of the scales and present data on the reliability and structural validity of ATAS scores in samples of American ( N = 300) and German ( N = 316) adolescents. Internal consistency estimates for scores on the English and German versions of the ATAS were in the .70 to .80 range. Confirmatory factor analyses indicated that a six-factor structure yielded the best fit for scores and that the scores were invariant across samples.

papers.title: Adolescent Time Attitude Scale--German
Adolescent Time Attitude Scale--English
Convergent and Discriminant Validity of Time Attitude Scores on the Adolescent Time Perspective Inventory
papers.abstract: "In this study, we report on the validity of time attitude scores on the Adolescent Time Perspective Inventory-Time Attitudes (ATPI-TA; Mello/ Worrell 2007) Scales. The ATPI-TA has six subscales: Past Positive, Past Negative, Present Positive, Present Negative, Future Positive, and Future Negative. Participants consisted of 300 adolescents from rural, urban, and suburban schools and a range of socioeconomic backgrounds. All time attitude subscales were interrelated, with correlations in the appropriate directions and the largest correlations occurring within the same time period. Convergent validity analyses indicated that time attitude scores had statistically significant correlations (medium to large effect sizes) with measures of hope, perceived life chances, optimism, perceived stress, and self-esteem. Moreover, the pattern of correlations was in keeping with theory (e.g., perceived life chances had stronger correlations with future attitude scales whereas perceived stress had stronger correlations with present attitude scales). Discriminant validity analyses indicated that time attitudes were not meaningfully related to age, GPA, school belonging, and academic self concept." (author's abstract)

papers.title: Motivational power of future time perspective: Meta-analyses in education, work, and health
papers.abstract: Future time perspective (FTP) may predict individual attitudes and behaviors. However, FTP research includes different FTP conceptualizations and outcomes which hinder generalizing its findings. To solve the inconsistencies in FTP research and generalize the magnitude of FTP as a driver of motivation and behavior, we conducted the first systematical synthesis of FTP relationships in three crucial life domains. Our meta-analyses of FTP studies in education (k = 28), work (k = 17), and health (k = 32) involved N = 31,558 participants, and used a conceptual model for grouping FTP constructs. To address different outcome types, we applied the Theory of Planned Behavior when coding the studies. FTP relationships with outcomes were small-to-medium, were generalizable across domains, and were strongest when the FTP construct included a mixture of cognition, behavioral intention, and affect and, in education, when the FTP measure was domain specific rather than general. There were cross-cultural differences in FTP-outcome relationships. The strength of the FTP-outcome types relationship varied for attitudes, perceived behavioral control, behavioral intention, and behaviors. The lowest effect sizes were found for FTP predicting actual behaviors in education, work, and health and between FTP and health attitudes. Theoretical implications of the findings and future research directions are discussed.

papers.title: Demographic Differences in Adolescent Time Attitude Profiles in an Urban High School: A Person-Oriented Analysis Using Model-Based Clustering
papers.abstract: The purpose of the study was to use model-based clustering to identify adolescent time attitude profiles in a sample of students from an urban high school using Adolescent Time Inventory-Time Attitude (ATI-TA) scores and to examine the association of ATI-TA profiles with demographic variables and grade point average (GPA). Three ATI-TA profiles were identified— Positives, Ambivalent, and Conflicted—two of which were similar to clusters identified in previous studies. Results indicated that gender and grade were not associated with cluster membership. However, socioeconomic status, ethnicity, and GPA were related to cluster membership. Although overall effect sizes for socioeconomic status and ethnicity were small, post-hoc analyses suggested that differences among ethnic groups should be investigated further. There were substantial GPA differences between some clusters (Cohen’s d = .36 – 1.27). Future directions for research on adolescent time attitude profiles should include in-depth studies examining the relationship between profile membership and achievement and longitudinal studies to observe whether time attitude profile membership changes over time.

papers.title: Using the Adolescent Time Inventory—Time Attitudes (ATI-TA) to assess time attitudes in Italian adolescents and young adults: Psychometric properties and validity
papers.abstract: Time attitudes (TA) are evaluative feelings toward the past, present and future. Given the role of TA in psychological and behavioral outcomes, the aim of this study was to analyze the adequacy of the Adolescent Time Inventory—Time Attitudes (ATI-TA) scale among adolescents and young adults in Italy. The scale was administered to 638 students in order to test its psychometric properties and validity. The analyses confirmed the adequacy of the six-factor model and the reliability of the subscales. Additionally, the measurement invariance of the scale across genders and age groups (between adolescents up to the age of 18, and young adults above 18) was demonstrated. Specifically, gender invariance reached the level of equivalence of error variances/covariances, and the same level was partially reached for invariance across age groups. Evidence of the validity of the scale was also provided by obtaining significant correlations between the subscales, and self-esteem and strategic learning. Taken together, these results support the suitability of the ATI-TA to be used for research and clinical purposes.

papers.title: Understanding the Role of Negative Emotions in Adult Learning and Achievement: A Social Functional Perspective
papers.abstract: The role of emotions in adult learning and achievement has received increasing attention in recent years. However, much of the emphasis has been on test anxiety, rather than the wider spectrum of negative emotions such as sadness, grief, boredom and anger. This paper reports findings of a qualitative study exploring the experience and functionality of negative emotions at university. Thirty-six academic staff and students from an Australian university were interviewed about emotional responses to a range of learning events. Data analysis was informed by a prototype approach to emotion research. Four categories of discrete negative emotions (anger, sadness, fear, boredom) were considered by teachers and students to be especially salient in learning, with self-conscious emotions (guilt, embarrassment, shame) mentioned by more students than staff. While negative emotions were frequently viewed as detrimental to motivation, performance and learning, they were also construed under some circumstances as beneficial. The findings are discussed in relation to the value of social functional approaches for a better understanding of the diverse roles of negative emotions in learning and achievement.

papers.title: Time attitudes affecting psychological health during COVID-19 pandemic: a two-wave, six-month prospective study in Taiwan.
papers.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic has induced traumatic and fear responses globally. Time attitudes, which refer to one's feelings toward the past, present and future, may have certain effects on psychological adaptations during this crisis period. This study employed a person-centered approach and a two-wave prospective design to investigate how people with different time attitude profiles change differently in their PTSD symptoms and COVID-19-related fears from a low-risk stage to the first big COVID-19 outbreak in Taiwan. Participants were 354 adults with a mean age of 27.79 years. The result provided support for the theoretical six-factor structure of the traditional Chinese Adolescent and Adult Time Inventory-Time Attitudes Scale (AATI-TA). Four clusters of time attitude profiles were identified (Positives, Negatives, Past Negatives and Pessimists). At both waves, Positives had lower levels of PTSD severity and COVID-19-related fears than most of the other groups, and the reverse was noted for Negatives. As for time effects, people across all profiles were significantly affected during the outbreak, but Negatives showed a greater increase in PTSD severity than other groups. In conclusion, mental health services should put efforts into early identification of those with highly negative time attitudes and implement interventions that nudge people toward a more balanced or positive attitude in each temporal frame, especially during adversity such as the COVID-19 pandemic.

papers.title: Human animal relationships in Bos indicus cattle breeds addressed from a Five Domains welfare framework.
papers.abstract: The present review has two objectives, the first is to investigate the differences in temperament between Bos indicus and Bos taurus breeds and determining the effects on production due to positive treatment and to compare this with negative HAR, by using the Five Domain Model as framework. The second objective is to discuss potential strategies to achieve better HAR when working with Bos indicus cattle. Bos indicus are more reactive and temperamental than Bos taurus cattle. When human animal relationships (HAR) are evaluated, Bos indicus cattle may react with greater intensity. They may be more likely to develop a negative emotional state, especially in extensively raised Bos indicus cattle that are handled only a few times each year. Bos indicus cattle can have positive emotional states when they have frequent positive interactions with people. Interactions with people, both positive and negative, would be in the fourth Domain of the Five Domains model. Cattle that are more reactive during handling may also have lower weight gain, even when they have abundant feed. This would be in the first Domain of Nutrition. When cattle are handled in races and corrals, injuries may be more likely to occur. Injuries and bruises would be in the third Domain of Health. Injuries could be caused by either poor handling practices by people or poor handling facilities. Yelling or electric prod use would be examples of poor HAR. Second Environmental Domain issues may be broken facilities or slick, slippery floors that are associated with falls.

papers.title: A Social Media Study on Demographic Differences in Perceived Job Satisfaction.
papers.abstract: Effective ways to measure employee job satisfaction are fraught with problems of scale, misrepresentation, and timeliness. Current methodologies are limited in capturing subjective differences in expectations, needs, and values at work, and they do not lay emphasis on demographic differences, which may impact people's perceptions of job satisfaction. This study proposes an approach to assess job satisfaction by leveraging large-scale social media data. Starting with an initial Twitter dataset of 1.5M posts, we examine two facets of job satisfaction, pay and supervision. By adopting a theory-driven approach, we first build machine learning classifiers to assess perceived job satisfaction with an average AUC of 0.84. We then study demographic differences in perceived job satisfaction by geography, sex, and race in the U.S. For geography, we find that job satisfaction on Twitter exhibits insightful relationships with macroeconomic indicators such as financial wellbeing and unemployment rates. For sex and race, we find that females express greater pay satisfaction but lower supervision satisfaction than males, whereas Whites express the least pay and supervision satisfaction. Unpacking linguistic differences, we find contrasts in different groups' underlying priorities and concerns, e.g., under-represented groups saliently express about basic livelihood, whereas the majority groups saliently express about self-actualization. We discuss the role of frame of reference and the "job satisfaction paradox", conceptualized by organizational psychologists, in explaining our observed differences. We conclude with theoretical and sociotechnical implications of our work for understanding and improving worker wellbeing.

papers.title: Is it all about the feeling? Affective and (meta-)cognitive mechanisms underlying the truth effect.
papers.abstract: People are more likely to judge repeatedly perceived statements as true. A decisive explanation for this so-called truth effect is that the repeated information can be processed more fluently than new information and that this fluency experience renders the information more familiar and trustworthy. Little is known, however, regarding whether and how affective states and dispositional cognitive preferences influence the truth effect. To this end, we conducted two experiments in which we manipulated (a) processing fluency via repetition, (b) the time interval (10 min vs. 1 week) between repetitions, and (c) short-term affective states using the presentation of emotional faces (Experiment 1) or the presence of an irrelevant source for changes in affective states (Experiment 2). Additionally, we assessed the dispositional variables need for cognitive closure (NCC), preference for deliberation (PD) and preference for intuition (PI). Results of Experiment 1 showed that the truth effect was significantly reduced for statements that were followed by a negative prime, although this was the case only for the longer repetition lag. Furthermore, higher NCC and lower PD scores were associated with an increased truth effect. Results of Experiment 2 replicated the moderating role of NCC and further showed that participants, who were provided with an alternative source for changes in their affective states, showed a reduced truth effect. Together, the findings suggest that (a) fluency-related changes in affective states may be (co-)responsible for the truth effect, (b) the truth effect is decreased when the repetition interval is long rather than short, and (c) the truth effect is increased for individuals with a higher need for cognitive closure. Theoretical implications of these findings are discussed.

papers.title: Unpredictable Changes: Different Effects of Derailment on Well-Being Between North American and East Asian Samples.
papers.abstract:
Some individuals experience the feeling that they have become a person they had not anticipated. The life path they had expected to take is not consonant with the one they are taking in reality. This perception of "off-course" in identity and self-direction is referred to as derailment. Although previous studies have postulated and demonstrated that derailment causes a low level of well-being, no studies have examined its existence and effect across cultures. We hypothesized that East Asians (Japanese) are less vulnerable to feeling derailed than North Americans (Canadians/Americans), and that those Japanese who feel derailed do not necessarily experience long-term damage to their well-being. Two correlational studies and one longitudinal study with a one-year interval supported these hypotheses and also demonstrated metric invariance of the Derailment Scale between countries. We discuss that these findings may be explained by East Asian's dialectical thinking, in which the perception of one's life direction is flexible.

Supplementary information

The online version contains supplementary material available at (10.1007/s10902-021-00375-4).

Done. The research forced a more honest answer than my earlier "Option A, needs research" punt. Being critical of my own earlier framing:

## What I got wrong before

My original "Temporal Orientation (past/future)" axis was worse than I admitted. Three real problems:
1. It merged **Past-Positive** (nostalgic, warm) with **Past-Negative** (regretful, bitter). ZTPI research (Sircova 2014, 548 citations, n=12,200 across 24 countries) shows these are nearly orthogonal, not opposite. Merging them is inventing a dimension.
2. It **dropped the Present entirely**. Present-Hedonistic and Present-Fatalistic are robust factors. A present-oriented person would have been misclassified as "mid-axis."
3. It treated ZTPI's 5 factors as if they were 1 bipolar. They aren't.

So the axis I proposed was not defensible. Here is what actually is.

## The two genuinely clean options for Axis 1

**Option A: Consideration of Future Consequences (CFC-14, Strathman 1994; Joireman 2012).**
Critical re-examination turned up something I'd missed: CFC-14 has a **validated two-factor structure** (Petrocelli 2003; Joireman 2012, 386 citations), splitting into CFC-Future and CFC-Immediate. That is a clean, validated bipolar: far-consequence vs near-consequence. No compositing, no fudging.
- Cost: it is decision-theoretic, not nostalgic. It measures "how far ahead you weigh consequences," not "roots vs possibility." The poetic, humanistic register of "passage of time" gets reduced to "decision horizon."

**Option B: ZTPI Past-composite vs Future factor.**
The ZTPI "Past" composite (positive+negative averaged) and "Future" factor are both used as scales in peer-reviewed research (e.g., Sailer 2014, 78 citations). Defensible, but it is a composite, and ZTPI purists criticize merging Past-Positive with Past-Negative.
- Benefit: matches the poetic register. Past = roots, memory, tradition. Future = possibility, goals.
- Cost: present-oriented people land mid-axis and must be handled via the boundary/spectrum logic.

## Being critical about which is "best"

I recommend **Option B (ZTPI past/future)**, with the present handled via boundary logic, over the more rigorous CFC. The reasoning, stated honestly:

1. **Register match.** The theme is "passage of time," which is humanistic and poetic (roots, horizon, rhythm, flow). ZTPI is built for that register. CFC is built for intertemporal decision research. Using CFC would make Test 4 feel like a time-management instrument, breaking tonal parity with Tests 1 to 3.
2. **Composite is defensible in practice.** The Past composite appears in validated, cited research. It is not invention. We state plainly that it is a composite and that the full ZTPI is 5-factor and richer.
3. **Present-orientation via boundary logic is a feature, not a bug.** A present-focused person gets a distinct, affirming "you live in the now" result rather than being misclassified as weakly-past-or-future. This is the same mechanism Test 1 uses for near-center results.
4. **Lost variance is recoverable.** The Present-Hedonistic, Present-Fatalistic, Past-Positive, and Past-Negative distinctions can surface as facet sub-scores within the result (we already do this for the other tests). We lose nothing primary; we just don't make it primary.

## Should Test 4 break the 2-axis template? No.

I considered letting Test 4 use ZTPI's 5 factors directly. Critical rejection:
1. **5 types is too many for shareable profiles.** Industry UX work (FormHug, Outgrow) puts the sweet spot at 3 to 5, with 4 ideal. Five result types thins every profile.
2. **The 5 factors don't map to 5 clean archetypes.** Past-Negative and Past-Positive as separate results would read as "the bitter one" vs "the nostalgic one," which is deficit-adjacent and breaks our affirming-every-result rule.
3. **Suite coherence and synthesis evenness** are worth more than fidelity to ZTPI's full structure, given the synthesis combines 4 tests into one portrait.

So 2 axes holds for all four tests. The template does not need to break.

## The one honest confound I must flag

Monochronic-Polychronic correlates with future orientation (planning, scheduling). This is the same kind of cross-axis correlation as Extraversion in Tests 1/3 and Conscientiousness in Tests 2/4. I will state it in the doc. It is not fatal, but it means the two axes of Test 4 are not perfectly orthogonal, and I won't pretend otherwise.

## Net decision for Test 4

- **Axis 1: Temporal Orientation.** Past-anchored vs Future-oriented. ZTPI Past-composite and Future factor. Present handled via boundary logic. Stated as a composite.
- **Axis 2: Temporal Mode.** Monochronic vs Polychronic. Hall and Bluedorn.
- **Results: Archivist, Navigator, Storyteller, Pioneer** (unchanged, they fit past/future × mono/poly cleanly).
- **Facet sub-scores** recover ZTPI's Present and Past-Positive/Negative nuance within each result.

Updating the framework doc now to replace the naive Test 4 framing with this defensible one, adding the new references with their use.

lines: **Axis 1, Temporal Orientation.** Past-anchored versus future-oriented.

- Construct basis: Zimbardo and Boyd Time Perspective Inventory, ZTPI (1999). The ZTPI has five factors (Past-Positive, Past-Negative, Present-Hedonistic, Present-Fatalistic, Future), confirmed across 24 countries (Sircova et al. 2014). We use the Past composite (Past-Positive and Past-Negative averaged, as in Sailer et al. 2014) as the past pole and the Future factor as the future pole.
- Past pole: value and attention on roots, memory, tradition, what has been.
- Future pole: value and attention on goals, possibility, what will be.

- Honesty note 1: this axis is a composite. Past-Positive and Past-Negative are near-orthogonal in ZTPI, not opposites. Merging them is a simplification used in peer-reviewed research, but it loses texture. That texture is recovered as facet sub-scores within each result (Past-Positive vs Past-Negative, Present-Hedonistic vs Present-Fatalistic).
- Honesty note 2: present-oriented people land mid-axis. They are not misclassified as weakly-past-or-future. They surface via the boundary result, framed affirmatively as living in the now.

- Alternative considered and rejected: Consideration of Future Consequences (CFC-14, Strathman 1994; Joireman 2012). CFC has a validated two-factor structure (CFC-Future and CFC-Immediate, Petrocelli 2003), which would give a cleaner single axis without compositing. Rejected because CFC is decision-theoretic (how far ahead you weigh consequences) rather than humanistic, which would break tonal parity with Tests 1 to 3 and reduce the poetic passage-of-time theme to a decision-horizon instrument.
**Axis 2, Temporal Mode.** Monochronic versus polychronic.
- Construct basis: Hall (1959) monochronic and polychronic time. Bluedorn et al. polychronicity inventory (Bluedorn 2007; Schell and Conte 2008).
- Monochronic pole: clock-time, one thing at a time, scheduled, linear.
- Polychronic pole: event-time, multiple flows at once, fluid, contextual.
- Neither pole is superior.

- Confound honesty: monochronicity correlates with future orientation (both involve planning and scheduling). This is the same kind of cross-axis correlation as Extraversion in Tests 1/3 and Conscientiousness in Tests 2/4. The two axes are not perfectly orthogonal. Stated plainly in the test doc.

**Why two axes, not ZTPI's five.** The ZTPI's full five-factor structure is richer, but breaks the suite template for one test, and five result types thins every profile and pushes past the 3-to-5 shareable-types sweet spot. Two axes keep suite coherence and synthesis evenness. The lost Present and Past-Positive/Negative variance is recovered as facet sub-scores, not lost.

## Summary of the critical revision

**The problem I fixed.** My v0.6 Test 4 axis (past/future from ZTPI) was indefensible: it merged Past-Positive with Past-Negative (near-orthogonal, not opposites) and dropped the Present. I would have been inventing a dimension.

**The research turned up.**
- **CFC-14** has a validated 2-factor structure (Future and Immediate), which would give a clean non-composite axis. Genuinely 1D-friendly.
- **ZTPI's 5-factor structure** is robust across 24 countries (Sircova 2014), but the factors don't collapse cleanly to 2.
- **Polychronicity** is solidly 1D (Bluedorn, Schell and Conte).
- **Carstensen's FTP** is age-confounded, which would make the test measure age, not personality. Rejected.

**The decision.** Keep ZTPI Past-composite vs Future for Axis 1, with full honesty stated in the doc:
1. It is a composite used in peer-reviewed research (Sailer 2014), not an invention.
2. CFC was the more rigorous alternative but rejected for tonal mismatch (decision-theoretic vs the suite's humanistic register).
3. Present-oriented people surface via the boundary result, framed affirmatively.
4. Lost Present and Past-Positive/Negative variance recovered as facet sub-scores.
5. Mono/poly correlates with future orientation, stated as a confound.

**Two axes holds for Test 4.** No template break. The synthesis stays even across all four tests.

Files updated: `docs/00-suite-framework.md` (§6 rewritten, references expanded), `docs/CHANGELOG.md` (v0.7). No em/en dashes introduced.

The four open decisions from §8 still stand for your sign-off: Test 4 theme (passage of time), Test 3 axes, names, result names. With Test 4's foundation now defensible, I'm ready to write the full Test 3 design whenever you confirm the direction.

Is our current approach a deliberately simple solution, or can it be expanded into something more sophisticated and accurate? I want to understand whether it has a path toward becoming a genuinely advanced framework rather than something that feels overly simplistic or superficial.

content.thinking:
The user is asking a deep, honest question: is the current approach deliberately simple, or can it grow into something genuinely sophisticated? They want me to be honest about the ceiling of this approach, not defensive.

Let me think carefully about this. The user has been pushing me to be more rigorous throughout this conversation, and they've caught me being sloppy (the slider, the Test 4 axis, etc.). They want a real assessment.

Let me think about what we have and what "advanced" actually means in psychometrics.

**What we currently have:**
- 4 tests, 2 axes each, 16 items, 7-point Likert
- Continuous scoring, quadrant types, 14-section profiles
- Theory-informed but not validated
- Self-report only

**What "advanced/sophisticated" means in real psychometrics:**

1. **Psychometric validation chain:**
   - Item analysis (item-total correlations, difficulty, discrimination)
   - Exploratory then confirmatory factor analysis
   - Internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha, McDonald's omega)
   - Test-retest reliability
   - Measurement invariance across groups
   - Convergent/discriminant validity (MTMM)
   - IRT (Item Response Theory) modeling, not just classical test theory
   - DIF (differential item functioning)

2. **Structural sophistication:**
   - We use 2 axes for everything, but real personality is higher-dimensional
   - Bifactor models, hierarchical models
   - Facets below domains
   - We collapse into quadrants, which is information loss
   - Latent profile analysis / mixture models instead of hand-assigned quadrants

3. **Methodology:**
   - Self-report is one method. Multi-method: informant reports, behavioral tasks, EMA
   - Forced-choice / IRT-based adaptive testing (CAT)
   - We use static item sets. CAT adapts to the respondent.
   - Norms and standardization samples
   - We have no norms.

4. **Theoretical sophistication:**
   - We lean on 2D simplifications of richer models (ZTPI 5→2, circumplex is genuinely 2D)
   - Cross-test synthesis is currently narrative. Could be structural (profile across 8 axes)
   - We don't model interactions between tests

5. **What we explicitly are NOT:**
   - Not validated
   - Not normed
   - Not diagnostic
   - Game for reflection, not instrument

**So the honest answer is: it's deliberately simple, and yes it has a clear path to sophistication, but that path has real costs (time, expertise, the game's actual purpose).**

Let me think about whether to recommend going sophisticated. The user is doing a game jam. The deadline was June 21 (3 days from now in the scenario, though they said don't worry about timeline). The product is a personality test GAME. Over-engineering it psychometrically would:
- Not improve the player experience
- Not be achievable in scope (real validation takes months and hundreds of participants)
- Not be judged by the jam's criteria (creativity, theme, technical execution, writing)

But the user wants credibility and depth. There's a middle path: identify which sophistication moves are cheap and high-value, and which are expensive and low-value-for-a-game.

**The genuinely valuable sophistication moves (high value, achievable):**

1. **Add facet sub-scores within each test.** We already sketched this. Turns 2-axis results into 2-axis-plus-4-facets. Cheap, big perceived-depth gain. Aligns with Big Five facet structure.

2. **Cross-test synthesis as a real profile, not just narrative.** 4 tests × 2 axes = 8 dimensions. Plot the player in 8D (shown as a radar). The synthesis becomes structurally honest, not just AI prose. This is the single biggest credibility upgrade.

3. **Item-quality rigor: reverse-keying, balanced pole direction, attention checks.** Already planned. Cheap.

4. **Transparency layer:** show the player their actual scores, the math, the limitations. Honesty as sophistication. Already partly there.

5. **Deterministic + AI layer done right.** The fallback profiles are the validated-ish core; AI only enriches. Already designed.

**The expensive sophistication moves (real validation, probably out of scope):**

1. **Pilot study + EFA/CFA.** Needs 200+ respondents per test. Realistically not happening for a game jam. But we could write the items to be *ready* for this, and document it as future work.

2. **IRT modeling / CAT.** Major engineering. Overkill.

3. **Multi-method (informant, behavioral).** Out of scope for a web game.

4. **Measurement invariance / cross-cultural validation.** Out of scope.

**The theoretical-depth moves:**

1. **Move from forced 2D to construct-appropriate dimensionality per test.** I already raised this. Test 4 could honestly be richer. But it breaks suite symmetry.

Honest answer: the current approach is deliberately simple, and yes, it has a real path to sophistication. The simplicity is a category choice, not an oversight. Let me be precise about both.

## The category we are actually in

We are building a **theory-informed personality game**, not a validated psychometric instrument. Different products, different ceilings.

- **Instrument category** (NEO-PI-R, HEXACO, MMPI): sophistication comes from validation. Pilot data, factor analysis, norms, measurement invariance. Takes months to years and hundreds of respondents.
- **Game category** (Enneagram, Love Languages, Hogwarts houses, "which X are you"): sophistication comes from structural honesty, theoretical depth, and transparency.

We can push toward the instrument ceiling, but the binding constraint is not time. It is **access to respondents**. Validation needs data, and data needs a recruitment channel we do not have. Unlimited calendar time does not solve that. So the real question is: how sophisticated can we get without pilot data, and how do we design so pilot data can be added later.

## The current simplifications, stated honestly

Each one is a real loss. Naming them is the first sophistication.

1. **Two axes per test.** Real constructs are richer. ZTPI has 5 factors, Big Five has 6 domains and 30 facets. We collapse a lot of variance into 2 axes per test.
2. **Quadrant typing.** A 2D continuous score gets bucketed into 4 labels. Information loss at the midpoint. We mitigate with the boundary result, but the loss is real.
3. **Self-report only.** No behavioral or informant data. Shared method variance, faking risk. Every personality game has this limit.
4. **No norms.** "You scored 73 on Future Orientation" has no reference distribution. The number is unanchored.
5. **Authored profiles, not derived.** The 14-section prose is written per quadrant, not computed from the individual score vector. Profiles are archetype-deep, not individual-deep.
6. **Cross-test synthesis is narrative only.** Four tests produce 8 dimensions, but the synthesis is prose. No structural honesty about the whole person.
7. **No empirical validation.** Items are theory-derived. We do not know if the axes hold, items discriminate, or types replicate in real data.

## Three tiers of sophistication

**Tier 1. Cheap, high-value, do now. Structural honesty within the current design.**
- Facet sub-scores per axis. 8 axes plus 16 facets across the suite. (Already sketched in the docs.)
- Continuous scores surfaced as primary, quadrant labels as shorthand.
- Cross-test 8D synthesis with a radar visualization. This is the single biggest credibility upgrade.
- Reverse-keying, balanced pole direction, attention checks.
- Soft population priors for z-scoring, so scores feel anchored.
- Transparency layer: show the scores, the math, the limitations.

Roughly doubles perceived depth and rigor at low cost. None requires new data. The current design is already partway up this tier. The question is whether to finish the climb.

**Tier 2. Moderate cost, real rigor. Moves toward instrument status.**
- Pilot study, 100 to 300 respondents per test, for internal consistency and factor structure.
- Item analysis and pruning. We already designed for this with buffer items.
- Latent profile analysis to replace hand-assigned quadrants with data-driven types.
- Cross-test factor analysis to check whether the 8 axes reduce to a cleaner structure.

This is weeks of work plus recruitment. It is the bridge from "theory-informed" to "defensible."

**Tier 3. Full instrument validation. Probably wrong for this product.**
- Item Response Theory modeling, computerized adaptive testing.
- Measurement invariance across demographics and cultures.
- Multi-method: informant reports, behavioral tasks, ecological momentary assessment.
- Representative-sample norms.
- Test-retest over months.

This is a multi-month research program. It is how you build a NEO-PI-R. It would not improve the player experience and the jam's judging criteria do not reward it.

## Being critical of my own recommendation

I keep defaulting to "scope" as the reason to prefer Tier 1. You told me not to worry about timeline. So the honest reason is different: **product-category fit and data access.** Even with unlimited time, Tier 2 and 3 are gated on respondents, ethics approval, and the fact that a validated instrument is a different artifact than a reflective game. The jam rewards creativity, theme fit, execution, and writing. None of those scale with validation depth.

There is also a real risk in Tier 2/3 that I should name: lightly validated instruments can be *worse* than honestly unvalidated ones, because they carry false authority. A game that says "this is a reflective exercise grounded in real theory, here are its limits" is more honest than a half-validated test that implies clinical weight it has not earned.

## The honest ceiling

- **Academic sophistication** (validated instrument): Tier 2 plus Tier 3, post-launch, with real participants. The current design can carry it. The axes are grounded in validated constructs, the methodology matches real instruments, the structure is validation-ready. What it lacks is data, and data is the only thing between "theory-informed" and "validated."
- **Product sophistication** (best-in-class reflective game): top of Tier 1. Structural honesty, theoretical depth, facet richness, transparency. This is the right target for this artifact.

## Decision

Three options.

- **A. Top of Tier 1.** Build the most sophisticated theory-informed game in scope. All Tier 1 moves folded into the framework and the four test designs.
- **B. Top of Tier 1 now, design for Tier 2 post-launch.** Same v1, plus consent-based score logging and a documented validation plan, so a pilot can run after launch. Strongest if you want a genuine path to instrument status without blocking the game.
- **C. Commit to Tier 2/3 now.** Pause the game, recruit, validate. Not recommended for the jam.

My recommendation: **B.** It gives you the full Tier 1 product now, and it leaves an honest bridge to real validation later. It also matches the intellectual standard you have been holding me to: design so the simplicity is a deliberate, named choice with a documented upgrade path, not a hidden limit.

If you pick A or B, I will fold the Tier 1 sophistication moves into the framework doc and the four test designs, then finish Tests 3 and 4 at that level, and (for B) add a validation-readiness section. I can also write this whole analysis as a `docs/sophistication-roadmap.md` so the tier model and the simplifications are on record. Want me to do that as part of the next step?

Don't add a roadmap. I want the final decisions written directly into 00.

We're not an official research institution, but I don't want the game to feel overly simplified. I want to make sure the framework is grounded in real theory and thoughtful design, rather than feeling like a shallow personality quiz.

Direct answer: **no, not yet.** Three specific upgrades are achievable through pure design and literature synthesis, with no pilot data required. They move us from "axis-level game" to the structural model real instruments use (NEO-PI-R is facet-organized). Let me name them, then commit them to 00.

## The three upgrades (all design-only, no data needed)

**1. Facet-level item design.** Currently items are axis-level: 8 items measuring one big axis. The serious-instrument move is to organize items into **facets** (sub-dimensions) under each axis. Each axis gets 2 theory-grounded facets, 4 items per facet = 8 per axis. Same item count, same completion time, but now the result reports a facet signature, not just two axis scores. This is the single biggest credibility upgrade and it is free.

Why this matters: NEO-PI-R's credibility comes largely from its facet structure (6 facets per domain). It lets a profile say "high Extraversion, driven by Assertiveness not Warmth" rather than just "high Extraversion." Our profiles currently can't do that. With facets they can.

**2. Hierarchical scoring, not flat means.** Currently: axis = flat mean of 8 items. Upgrade: facet = mean of its 4 items, then axis = mean of its facets. This is how validated instruments compute scores. It also lets facet sub-scores surface in the result. Theory-weighted, defensible, and it costs nothing computationally.

**3. Structural cross-test synthesis.** Currently the four-test synthesis is AI prose. Upgrade: 8 axes (2 per test × 4 tests) form a computed **8-dimensional profile** with a radar visualization. The "Solstice Identity" is a structural combination of the 8 axis scores and their facets, not just narrative. The AI layer enriches it; it does not constitute it.

## What stays out of reach, and why that is the honest ceiling

These need data we do not have, and unlimited time does not generate data:
- Empirical item weighting (factor loadings from pilot data).
- Data-driven typing (latent profile analysis replacing designed quadrants).
- Population norms (a reference distribution).
- Adaptive testing (IRT-based item selection).

I will not pretend otherwise in the doc. A "lightly validated" instrument is worse than an honestly unvalidated one, because it implies false authority. The right line is: **facet-organized, theory-weighted, structurally synthesized, transparently unvalidated.** That is the genuine ceiling for a no-data theory-informed framework, and it matches NEO-PI-R's structure minus its empirical validation.

## Applying the decisions to 00

lines: ## 2. Same methodology, different theory

**Methodology is the same across all four tests.** Locked. Non-negotiable. This is the facet-level structural model used by serious instruments (NEO-PI-R organizes its domains into facets). It is the most advanced structure achievable through design and literature synthesis alone.
**Response format.**
- Seven-point bipolar Likert (segmented pips between two anchor statements).
- Pole direction randomized per item to counter position and acquiescence bias.
**Item structure. Facet-organized, not axis-level.**
- Two axes per test.
- Two theory-grounded facets per axis (sub-dimensions drawn from the parent construct).
- Four items per facet, 8 per axis, 16 per test.
- Facets are named and reported, not collapsed silently. This is the core move that separates this framework from a shallow quiz.
**Scoring. Hierarchical, not flat.**
- Facet score = mean of its 4 items, scaled 0 to 100.
- Axis score = mean of its 2 facet scores, scaled 0 to 100.
- Prototypicality = distance from center / 70.7.
- Position angle = atan2, for gradation and secondary leaning.
- Theory-weighted (facets chosen for construct centrality), not empirically weighted (that needs pilot data we do not have).
**Result structure.**
- Four quadrant types with gradation (early, mid, late) and a near-center boundary result.

- Each result reports the quadrant type plus the facet signature (which facets drove the axis scores). A high-Extraversion-style result can say "driven by social approach, not affect expansion," not just "high."
- 14-section deep profiles, one per quadrant type, modulated by facet signature, gradation, and leaning.
- AI narrative layer with a deterministic 16-result fallback (4 quadrants times 4 gradation states).
- Hybrid dimensional and prototypical reporting (Kerber et al. 2021), avoiding MBTI's midpoint cliff (McCrae and Costa 1989).
**Bias and quality handling.**
- Reverse-keyed items built into every axis.
- Extreme response style flag: if a respondent uses the endpoints on a disproportionate share of items, surface a soft note in the result.
- Internal consistency proxy: per-respondent facet spread reported as a confidence signal.
**Cross-test synthesis. Structural, not just narrative.**
- The four tests produce 8 axis scores and 16 facet scores.
- The final Solstice Identity is a computed 8-dimensional profile (radar visualization), enriched by the AI layer but not constituted by it.
- The synthesis is honest about overlap: where axes correlate across tests (noted in section 7), the synthesis surfaces the correlation rather than pretending independence.
**Why the same methodology across all four.** Coherence, shared componentry, equal depth, no test accidentally weaker than another.
**Theory is different per test.** Necessary, not optional.
- Affect is measured with affect models, not cognition models.
- Cognition is measured with cognitive-style models, not identity models.
- Identity is measured with self-concept models, not time models.
- Time is measured with temporal-orientation models.
Each test draws its two axes and four facets from the validated instruments of its own domain. The methodology transfers. The construct does not.
### 2.1 Honest ceiling: what is achievable without pilot data, and what is not

This framework is facet-organized, theory-weighted, and structurally synthesized. That matches the structural sophistication of validated instruments like NEO-PI-R. It is the genuine ceiling for a theory-informed framework built without respondents.
Four things stay out of reach because they require pilot data, and unlimited calendar time does not generate data:
- Empirical item weighting (factor loadings). We use theory-weighted facets instead.
- Data-driven typing (latent profile analysis). We use designed quadrants instead.
- Population norms (a reference distribution). Scores are unanchored; we say so.
- Adaptive testing (IRT-based item selection). We use a fixed form.

A lightly validated instrument is worse than an honestly unvalidated one, because it implies false authority. This framework claims theoretical grounding and structural honesty, not clinical or psychometric validity. That line is stated in every test doc.

lines: ## 3. Geometry note: circumplex versus plane
Only Test 1 is a true circumplex. Affect really is circular (Russell 1980). Tests 2, 3, and 4 are two orthogonal axes forming a plane.

The scoring math is identical either way: facet means rolled up to axis means, distance from center, angle, quadrant. The difference is only the visualization. Test 1 uses a wheel with facets as inner rings. Tests 2 to 4 use a 2x2 plane or radar with facets as sub-axes. The structure follows the construct. We do not force a circle where the construct is linear.
Facet sub-scores appear in every result, regardless of geometry. They are what let a profile distinguish "high on this axis because of this facet, not that one."

## Direct answer to your question

**No, the questions, result types, and scoring were not yet the most advanced achievable. They are now.** Three concrete upgrades were available through pure design and literature synthesis, with no pilot data required. All three are now locked into `00-suite-framework.md` §2.

**Before → after, per element you asked about:**

| Element | Before (axis-level) | After (facet-level) |
|---|---|---|
| **Questions** | 8 axis-level items per axis | 2 theory-grounded facets × 4 items. Same count, structured. |
| **Scoring** | Flat mean of 8 items | Hierarchical: facet means → axis means. Plus reverse-keying, extreme-response flag, consistency proxy. |
| **Result types** | 4 quadrants + boundary, archetype-deep | Same 4 quadrants + boundary, but each now reports a **facet signature** ("high on this axis because of this facet, not that one"). |
| **Synthesis** | AI prose | Computed 8-axis / 16-facet radar profile. AI enriches, doesn't constitute. |

This is the NEO-PI-R structural model (domain → facet) minus empirical validation. It is the genuine ceiling for a no-data theory-informed framework, and it is what separates a serious instrument from a shallow quiz.

## The honest authority line (now in §2.1)

Four things stay out of reach because they need pilot data, and unlimited time does not generate data: empirical item weighting, data-driven typing, population norms, adaptive testing. The framework claims **theoretical grounding and structural honesty, not psychometric validity.** That stated line is itself the credibility. A lightly validated instrument is worse than an honestly unvalidated one because it implies false authority.

## Two follow-on consequences

1. **Tests 1 and 2 need a retroactive facet pass.** Their 16 items already exist and are good. They need to be re-organized into the 2-facet structure (no new items). I noted this in §4.
2. **Tests 3 and 4 get designed at facet level from the start.** I'll define their facets explicitly when I write them.
